p: [interposing] Okay.
Decline and that tracks to when that new plan went into effect.
Alright. And domestic violence, is that up, down, and how are we doing with it?
Domestic violence is up.
I know.
And we have just done– completed a massive reorganization of the Department to address it. Domestic violence isn’t just up this year. This has been really since–
[interposing] But it’s good in a sense people are reporting which is the other thing.

But it’s up meaningfully since I would say the pandemic, and we have just completed a massive reorganization of the Department so that we can better address not only the crime, but improve how we deal with victims. And so a lot of that reorganization has been about one, improving the quality and the focus on DV investigations; two, doing a better job of hunting down DV perps; and three, is making sure that if you are a victim of domestic violence, you are not getting outreach from multiple different officers all asking you the same information, that we streamline who talks to victims and about what.
And it’s making a difference, you think, in terms of numbers or how is it going to impact–
[interposing] I think–
[interposing] Or it’s too soon to know?

I think that it will make a difference. I think it already has made a difference

in terms of the way we treat victims. We are now taking a victim-centered approach to domestic violence. Whether to the extent that it will bring DV numbers down, I don’t know. What I can tell you is those cases will be investigated in a more streamlined and effective and victim-centered way.
Okay. Thank you. And then finally just paperwork. I know– I mean, can you help– we know that there’s still a lot. Is it changing? I know we’ve talked about this in the past. If you–
[interposing] So, there’s a lot of paperwork.
There is.
There is too much paperwork.
Yes.

I actually find like the paperwork issue in the past has gotten politicized. Like, this is not a political statement. There’s too much paperwork that the NYPD has to do, and I would love to work with this Council on streamlining it if the Council is open to it, both the paperwork and the general reporting requirements on this Department. Just requires a lot of resources to meet.

So, there’s reporting and then there’s if I have a broken window in my car– which I don’t have a car, but if I had one then I go to the precinct. Is that still a paper-mandated report or is that online?
Well, any crime– any crime com– when I say paperwork, I don’t mean crime–
[interposing] There’s two kinds. Yeah, there’s the reporting and then there’s the paperwork that we citizens have to fill out when we have a crime situation and that the officers have to fill out.
So, we have digitized a number of the forms that our officers have to fill out. The– over the past I don’t know, seven years, there are some that are still done on paper.

Okay. And can you get us a list of those? Or I’m not asking for more reporting. I do think that when you finish your tour, because we did go out with some tours, there’s still a lot of paperwork to be done. Can– and that perhaps could also be streamlined. And maybe we can help you do that. If there's too much reporting there.
I agree. I’m going to look forward to it. Thank you very much Council Member.
Thank you very much, Commissioner.

And thank you, Council Member Brewer. Next we’ll hear from Council Member Nurse and then from Majority Leader Shaun Breau. I also want to recognize that we’ve been joined by Council Member Justin Sanchez and Avilés.

Thank you, Chair. Good morning, Commissioner. I just have three questions. You’ve done some outreach recently about police communications technicians. It looks like their starting salary is from $42-$49,000 per year, and I think– it’s been communicated to me that very experienced folks are about $60,000 per year. Has there been any effort to bring that salary up?

So, unfortunately, the salaries for all of these positions are not really set by the agency. They are set through collective bargaining agreements that are largely led by the Office of Labor Relations. However, we have worked very closely with the union and Henry to do things to try to make the position more financially appealing

to applicants including how we administer this bonus that was put in a few years ago to make it so that more people are eligible for it, so it becomes a part of the general salary.

Yeah. And some of the concerns were because of the low salary, high turnover– and I understand you’re not directly in charge of it, but I’m putting it out here for the public. Low wages, high turnover, people are saying they’re frequently mandated to do 16-hour shifts very often.

Less than– too much, but less and less. So what was going on at 911 was that it basically wasn’t managed as far as I can tell. What I saw when I came in a year ago and looked at it was an unacceptably high number of call-taking delays, not because the police communications technicians weren’t doing their job, but because their managers weren’t allocating the staffing based on when calls come in. You know what time of day the most calls come in, and that's when our staffing was the lowest. And so there were a number of things that we were able to do working with the union on, you know,

12-hours, 10-hour tours, 8-hour tours, making sure we had the right number of squads working at the right time to not only improve our service to the public, but to I would say meaningfully bring down some of the forced overtime. But there still is quite a fair amount of it.

Fair enough. And then– just you had a lot in your testimony about international incidents. How many NYPD personnel are deployed outside the United States, and do you have a cost of that international–
[interposing] so, it's 12 countries, and the New York City Police Foundation picks up the cost associated with it, everything except, of course, the officer’s salary.
And what is that budget?
The–
[interposing] The budget of the cost of personnel overseas that is carried by the–
[interposing] Oh, for the 12 officers?
Yeah, so the portion that the foundation pays for is $1.26 million a year.
And sorry, you’re saying 12 countries–
[interposing] The salary–
[interposing] Is that 12 officers?
Yes, yes. And so it would be the–
It’s 12 salaries.

Okay. And then for the Q Team, what– just two more questions. How has the NYPD’s role changed in relationship to the new encampment policy that was announced, and how does the Q Team fit within that, given that at least what it’s reported is they do some work related to encampment?

So, under the Adams Administration, the New York City Police Department, I would say- it’s fair to say, the Mayor’s Office with the NYPD is the lead agency. It was like the lead among the three different agencies involved. That would be NYPD, DHS, and Sanitation. And what that would mean is when the complaint would come in, we would be the first to respond, and then only later go jointly with the other three agencies. This new

administration is– has made a policy decision that the NYPD should not be the first agency to respond, but instead that should be the Department of Homeless Services, and so that’s the main change in how this administration responds to homeless encampment issues.
Okay. And what are the top complaints from the Q Team? What are your top three complaints that you’re constantly responding to?

Oh, we have it here, but I can probably do it off the top of my head. Yep. Illegal parking, residential noise, street sidewalk noise, and blocked driveway. Then abandoned vehicle. Then encampments. But like to give you a sense, illegal parking last year was 577,000. Residential noise was 463,000. Blocked driveway was 172,000. Abandoned vehicles, which we’ve made a lot of progress on since our Sanitation days working on it, is almost 68,000.
And last question. What is a normal tenure of a precinct commander?
Oh, Chief LiPetri can answer that. He has a lot of thoughts about it.

So, since I became Chief of Department in October, I have asked the Chief of Patrol to really try and limit to have less than two years as a precinct commander. There are case-to-case– there are cases that the commander might be there less than two years, but we really want that two years obviously for the community, for the officers, and also you know, the experience.
So, at least two years.

At least two. Yeah, I feel like– and I’ll just– I mean, I don’t have problems with my commanders, but at the 83rd I feel like we’ve just had a string of turnover. I think I’ve had four in my four years and three months I’ve been here, and think that’s a little bit of a problem, so what do you–
[interposing] I can–

[interposing] How do you all look into when you’re seeing these high rates of turnover? What is your institutional response to looking and examining a precinct or the policies that, you know– a promotion and things like that-that might be pulling people out of these roles?

The Chief can speak to the specifics of it, but I think that you both are going to be quite aligned on this, because when the Chief was named Chief of Department, he really took a leadership role. He decides who the precinct commanders are, and one of the things he called out immediately was this issue of turnover. People are not staying in their commands long enough. It’s not good for the community. It’s not good for the cops, and frankly it’s not good for the individual. So, that is something that the Chief also identified and that I think has been addressed since he now approves any precinct commander that enters or exits. Do you have anything to add to that, Chief?
No, ma’am.

Well, it would be good to maybe an– I’m done, Chair, but if you could outline it here or send us some– how has it been addressed other than you might not approve it, but what are some of the outcomes or analysis that you had when reviewing that?

Well, I don’t really– I’d like to get you any information that you want, but I

would say that most of it, all of it, was how it was managed, right? People moving into different roles, especially leadership roles in the Department like overtime is a very basic management function of an organization, and so how long someone was serving as a precinct commander wasn’t something that was managed to or against. And so like other things in the Department, it got out of control. And now, we’ve set very clear standards. Like, for example, like we want people to be precinct commanders for at least two years. There are certain commands that are only a second command or a third command, and we’re actually sticking to those things and managing against them.
Thank you, Chair. Thank you.

Thank you so much. Next we’ll hear from Council Member Alexa Avilés. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Pleasant surprise. I thought I was much further in the queue. Thank you, Chair. Thank you everyone for being here. I guess I wanted to start with if you could provide for me, obviously not here, but just to make the request for–

I cover the 72nd, 76, 78, 66, and one other that I’m forgetting and I’m sorry. The number of authorized and uniformed officers–
[interposing] We will do that. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: For those precincts. And I have to congratulate two officers who delivered a baby the other day in the 72nd precinct.
Happens more than you think. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: [interposing] A gift. A gift–
[interposing] They’re amazing. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: To our community.

We should always remember that. They’re a gift to our communities. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: For– to shift over to the topic of immigration. I just want to flag for the Department, and thank you for the meetings that we have had over a certainly the year, this past year. There is still an outstanding communication that I’m waiting for a response to, a letter that I submitted in August, and re-upped. So, just waiting for those responses.
Sure. Though I will point out that I believe that subsequent to that meeting we actually met, myself, the Police Commissioner, you, other members of the Council. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Yes.

And then Speaker. We actually sat with you and answered every question you had on the subject of immigration. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So, I think there’s a little confusion around the timing of that. We did seat– we sat together. We had productive meetings. This was questions that suffered– weird freudian slip, questions that emerged from that meeting that we sent after.
We will make sure to get back to you on– COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: [interposing] So, I just want to flag.

I apologize that if we have outstanding correspondence, my office will circle back with yours to make sure we’re responding to the correct questions and get you those answers.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Yeah. I’m not Gale Brewer. Council Member gets a response immediately from every agency in New York City. No, I’m teasing. In terms of immigration, I think one of the questions that I really would love to hear for the record and certainly would love to hear you, Commissioner, provide a directive is are there any circumstances under which NYPD would be wearing any other uniform besides its NYPD uniform?

Fewer and fewer. Obviously, the vast majority of the Police Department wears the blue pants, blue shirt. Well, wears the standard uniform of the day. We obviously have certain units that work plain clothes and that have to work plain clothes based on what their assignments are. But one of the things that we’re doing is to the extent possible, to the extent the work allows for it, we are trying to– we are getting units to standardize uniforms. So, one great example is our CRT Unit used to wear a special khaki pants. They no longer wear their special khaki pants. They now wear blue pants. And so we’re trying to get as many officers and units

as possible where the work allows for it to wear the standard uniform. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: So, I understand the plain clothes units. Are there any circumstances where NYPD would be wearing vests that say just police, just HSI?
No, we would never wear HSI vests, and we would never wear– I don’t think vests that just say police. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Generic?
Chief, do you know? Can you think of anything?
I cannot think of an outer NYPD vest that just says police. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay.
And Chief, just to confirm, NYPD would not wear HSI vests? We’d wear NYPD vests?
Absolutely not. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: And that would be for any other agency other than–
[interposing] Correct. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: They would never have DEA or some other agency’s–

[interposing] No.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Anything on them? Okay.

That is correct. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: In terms of– just to wrap up this particular question, I think– my understanding is the policy is when residents ask police officers for their name and badge on an interaction, that officers are supposed to respond to them. Is that correct?
Yes. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay.

Yes. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Because we have seen– I’ve several instances and I will send it to your office where officers were asked and this in the context of also people thinking they were immigration. So, asking them to identify themselves because they’re wearing plain clothes but with obviously hanging badges, and got in a car and left.

So, if you let us know– certainly, lots of people report those types of violations to CCRB, but you’re also welcome to send it to us if you’d like some training and reinstruction. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Yeah, yeah. So, I think–

[interposing] But that is a violation of Department policy. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you. Thank you. That’s what I understood, and obviously my constituents understand that as well, and we're very dismayed that– also an instance of like shoving, just pushing people and– so I will follow up with you.
Thank you. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: I think I’m out of time, but thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Avilés, and we’ll have a second round of questions as well. And just to follow up on that issue, is that a Department policy or is that city law?
About?
The rule requiring that they identify theirselves, provide a badge number?
Go ahead, Michael.
It is an NYPD policy as far as providing your shield number and your name. I do not know if it’s a city–

[interposing] And it’s certainly a city law. For example, obstruct your name and badge number, there’s actually a city

law that speaks to that. Separate and apart from the business card issue, there’s a city law that speaks to the fact that NYPD officers are not permitted to obstruct their badge number.

Okay. Thanks for that information. So, I have a few more questions. Want to go back to the topic of headcount and overtime, but actually before that we’ll go back to the policy-related questions. Want to go back to the topic of the Department of Community Safety. Anything that you can share on that? I mean, we’ve heard a lot about that specific title, but other than the title, we’ve heard very little to no specifics? Is there any information that you could share about how this Department can potentially work?

I would generally refer you to the Mayor’s Office. And just add the numbers that I provided previously, which is in New York City in calendar year 2024 we had about 4.3 million 911 calls for service at the NYPD. Of those, 85,793 were non-violent calls for people in mental health crisis, i.e., they would be eligible for today’s B-HEARD program. That means that roughly two percent of the 911 calls for service

today would be eligible for non-police response under the B-HEARD program as it exists.

The final question on the issue of policy, this one is about sound decibels. Many of us have started having conversations about how loud emergency vehicles can be, not only police cars, but also, you know, fire trucks. V I mean, they should be loud, but a big question is how loud should they be so that they could accomplish their goal of notifying people around them. I mean, as we know, excessive siren noise decreases quality of life, increases stress, anxiety, but also it could be ineffective. If people from our community hear the same exact noise every three seconds, it’s going to be ineffective.

[interposing] That’s where all my stress and anxiety comes from. I wasn’t able to place it. Thank you. We are very happy to look at that issue with you. I, obviously, have been tracking the issue for the past several years as it relates to the Fire Department, and I know that Council Member Brewer led efforts there, but happy to talk to you about it.
Right. And based on the research they’ve done and everything they– all the conversations you’ve had, NYPD has– is it 120 decibels?
We’re happy to have follow up meetings and provide you all the information you need, but I don’t have our decibel level here.

And final question on policy. One of my former colleagues, now Senator Eric Bottcher, introduced a bill that would require social workers in police precincts. Do you think this would be a good idea, at least in the precincts that have the highest amount of mental health issues, and youth-related challenges?

No, we are– actually as a department we do have programs that involve social workers, in particular our call response work that our– Alex Crohn, our Deputy Commissioner of Strategic Initiatives can tell you about.

Yeah. So we pair NYPD police officers with clinicians from DOHMH. The’s about 16 officers that are assigned to that unit, and they respond not to 911 calls, but rather visit people they know are most in need of services.

So, they do identify the people with most severe mental illness who might need services. So, that exists already. And of course, in the precincts we do have the crime victim advocates who are able to provide crime victim services. So we do a lot of this work already.

Alright, sounds good. And on the siren issues, decibel issue, look forward to continuing that conversation. I actually moved to another side of my building. It’s next to a road, and yeah, during the day we cannot open the window because every three seconds it’s a firetruck, an ambulance, and etcetera, and of course we need to make sure that people are notified. But the big question is how much noise is needed. The next question is whether if members of our community hear the same exact noise every three seconds, whether they even process the noise once they hear it again.
Understood.
And therefore making it ineffective.
I just know that fire truck and ambulance is not the NYPD, but no–
Right, yeah, of course, yeah.
And I’m going to look forward to it.

Alright, sounds good. Going back to the headcount topic and forced overtime, and also recruitment and retention. Based on the conversations you’ve had, I know you mentioned the union and the officers are in the best position to answer to this. But based on the conversations that you’ve had and the information that you gained, what are the top reasons that police officers usually leave the force?

Leave the force, do we have that data here? I'm not sure we have here right now the exit interview reasons for leaving. I can tell you that less one percent of our uniformed members leave for other Police Departments annually.
Less than one person for other Police Departments. How many police officers have left the Department and how many have we gained? Can you provide data for the last three years?
I think we did this one already, but I’m happy to redo it. Hold on.
And also, how many separations have been due to retirement versus other reasons?
Yeah. I have that in here. Let me just find it. Okay. Separations from officers retiring compared to officers leaving the force before retirement, that’s what you want to know?
Yes.

Historically 10 percent of our class hires will leave by their first year of service, 30 percent by their fifth year of service, 70 percent by their 20th year of service, and 90 percent by their 25th year of service.
Nice data. How many police officers have left the Department, though, and how many have we gained? Can you provide actual numbers for the last three years?

Okay. In– I can give you the net numbers. So, in calendar year ‘25, we added– we were net up. We added 758 officers. In calendar year ‘24 we added 12 officers, and in calendar year ‘23 we lost 280 officers.
Alright. Good job with the hiring and the–
[interposing] Thank you. Thank you. We really tried very hard.

And talk to us about their tenure. How long– actually, no you already provided information that kind of answers that. This is all public info, but still to good have this on the record. Talk to us about the salary of police officers. What’s the starting salary?
Starting– yeah. Starting salary is $55,942, and after a year and a half it goes up to $57,976, with increases each year reaching $109,352 after five and a half years.
And what’s the average salary considering the 300 hours that they generally do in overtime. Would you say we add an additional like $30,000 to that starting salary?
For calendar year 2025 on average officers earned approximately $26,000 overtime per year. So with an average salary of $103,000, that would total $129,000.

Talk to us about the police response time for different crimes. vWhat’s the

average response for shootings, homicides, domestic violence, assaults, and anything else that–

[interposing] Okay. We track two different things, crimes in progress meaning a robbery that’s in– well, crimes in progress and then serious crimes in progress. So, for the first four months of fiscal year 2026, response times for serious crimes in progress, which is many of the ones you’re talking about, are down 48 seconds, and response times for all crimes in progress are down six seconds. But the crimes that you are– said, were mostly the serious crimes in progress. So that’s down 48.

Okay. Going back to the overtime issue. How much of a role does headcount play on the issue of overtime? I know you mentioned generally it’s a few hours of overtime. They have to do paperwork or finalize their day. How much does headcount, though, play a role on that issue?

Less of a role than you think. So, let’s talk about one area where we really– we often need overtime and that is for like a detail or a big event, or a parade. That parade and that– doesn’t happen every single day. So you don’t

need to hire an extra officer to work every day for a parade that’s going to happen like once a month or a few times a month, etcetera. So, there– it is related, but not directly correlated.
Okay. I’ll pause now. I’ll call Council Member Hanks who was with us earlier today. Had to leave for a hearing that she had across the street. Council Member Hanks, the floor is yours.
Good afternoon.
Good afternoon.

Thank you. First, I want to thank Commissioner Tisch and the team here for your thorough and informative testimony this morning. I want to thank you and the members of NYPD for their service and truly the important job that they do in helping keep New Yorkers safe. So, I wanted to– I have questions in a few spaces, apologies, because I didn’t think I was going to get called on that fast.
That’s the theme today.

Really quickly on the uniform headcount reduction. I know this has been talked about for most of the hearing. But specifically with Staten Island, how many uniform

officers are assigned to Staten Island today versus prior years, and will Staten Island lose officers under the 300 position reduction plan?
